hardening.observed: MEASURED on disk: all three legacy release projects (data/stripe.com/release-projects/stripe.com-2026-08-19T06-36-35-798Z, data/linear.app/release-projects/linear.app-2026-08-25T23-32-42-075Z, .../linear.app-2026-08-25T23-54-21-435Z) record stageStatus.template.artifact.excluded = [".next","node_modules","out"] and stageStatus.content.artifact.excluded = [].
hardening.decision: (b) emit an explicit operator warning — NOT (a) refresh the recorded set on load.
hardening.reasoning: src/release/freshness.ts:296-299 re-hashes with the RECORDED set, so the recorded hash only has meaning UNDER that set. Swapping the current set in during adaptReleaseProject would reinterpret a hash computed under the old one: every one of the six recon-template run dirs already contains report/, so those bytes are folded into the recorded template hash today. Adopting the new set would make the recomputed hash differ immediately, turning three projects that build fine right now into projects a frozen-stage refusal (build.ts:164) bricks at LOAD time, with no operator action and no way to opt out. That trades a latent, action-triggered risk for a certain, unconditional break. Option (a) could only be made safe by verifying recorded == recomputed-under-new-set first, which requires disk I/O inside adaptReleaseProject — today a pure, synchronous, read-never-writes function (src/release/instance.ts:126-160). Historical hash immutability (Tasks 23-26) also forbids rewriting the hash itself. So the residual risk is SURFACED rather than hidden or silently 'fixed'.

hardeningCorrections.defect: src/release/prepare.ts (pre-correction :258-259) chose `carried !== undefined && !frozen ? carried.artifact : lineageArtifact`. For every executable stage the CARRIED ArtifactRef (with its old `excluded`) was kept and the freshly re-hashed lineage ref was discarded, so the content stage could never pick up CONTENT_DERIVED_HASH_EXCLUSIONS. The warning at src/release/freshness.ts:150-152 tells the operator to `pnpm release:prepare --project-id <id>`; doing so changed nothing and the warning persisted forever.

fix.code:
const samePath = carried?.artifact != null && carried.artifact.path === lineageArtifact.path;
const artifact = carried !== undefined && !frozen && !samePath ? carried.artifact : lineageArtifact;
fix.shape: Adopt the freshly re-hashed lineage ref when the carried artifact IS the lineage artifact (same path). The carried ref is still preferred whenever the paths differ.

hardeningCorrections.whyWideningThePickupPastFrozenStagesIsSa: The comment at prepare.ts:255-257 scopes the pickup to frozen stages for ONE reason: an executable stage that a release:build rerun advanced points at a NEW run dir the accepted lineage does not know about, and adopting the lineage there would silently revert the project to the pre-rerun artifact (asserted by the pre-existing check 27.35). That risk is entirely a PATH-DIVERGENCE risk. Guarding on `carried.artifact.path === lineageArtifact.path` preserves it exactly: a diverged stage still keeps its carried ref (proved by 27H.7f and by 27.35, both of which FAIL under an unguarded 'always adopt lineage' — negative control 5). When the paths are equal the two refs describe the SAME bytes on disk and differ only in how they were hashed, so adopting is a re-hash in place, not an artifact swap: id and path are unchanged (asserted by 27H.7e).

hardeningCorrections.honestTradeoff: A re-prepare now re-baselines a non-frozen artifact that sits at the SAME path as the accepted lineage. If an operator hand-edited bytes in that run dir and then ran release:prepare, the stage's own 'artifact bytes drifted' signal is re-baselined instead of raised (downstream stages still stale, because their recorded inputsHash was computed against the old artifact hash). This is inherent: prepare is defined as 'recomputes every ArtifactRef from disk' (prepare.ts:9-10), and re-hashing and drift-detecting the same directory are the same number. A drift-guard that refused to adopt when the carried hash no longer matched was considered and REJECTED: the legacy content dir's old hash folded report/ bytes in, so a single `pnpm content:qa` run makes it 'drifted' under the carried set and the guard would have blocked the very re-hash MAJOR 1 is about — the remedy would still never clear.

planCascadeFix.agent: Task 27 — Release Plan Cascade Fix (follow-up to the real-data release exercise)
planCascadeFix.objective: Make release:plan agree with release:build about the same project by giving the dependency-cascade fixpoint ONE implementation, decide and record what the persisted stageStatus stores, stop a resolution field that matches no requirement from vanishing, and correct one prose count in the exercise handoff.

defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.symptom: release:plan printed "READY (fresh): … theme, seo, production" while release:build --dry-run printed "WOULD RUN content, theme, seo, production" for the same project state (a resolution applied, nothing rebuilt yet). The persisted stageStatus carried the same un-cascaded view.
defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.rootCause: The staleness fixpoint was inlined in buildRelease only (src/release/build.ts, pre-fix lines 109-126). refreshStageStatuses returned RAW per-stage freshness, so plan.ts, resolve.ts and prepare.ts — the three other readers, two of which PERSIST what they get — never saw the cascade.
defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.fix: Extracted the fixpoint verbatim into `propagateStaleStages` (src/release/freshness.ts:367) and call it from INSIDE refreshStageStatuses (src/release/freshness.ts:343). The inline loop in build.ts is deleted, not duplicated: the cascaded view is now the only view any reader can obtain, so the surfaces cannot drift apart by omission again. The function is exported so a future caller that legitimately needs it (e.g. a reader that assembles StageStatus without a refresh) reuses it rather than re-deriving it.
defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.singleSourceProperty: There is exactly one `status = "stale"` cascade assignment in src/release/**; `grep -n propagateStaleStages src/release/*.ts` returns the definition (freshness.ts:367), its single call site (freshness.ts:343) and one comment reference in build.ts:113. No call site can opt out, because it runs inside the only function that produces StageStatus records from a project.
defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.buildBehaviourUnchanged: The fixpoint is idempotent over a DAG and it now runs immediately before the point build used to run it (same input: the just-refreshed statuses, before applyBlocking). buildRelease's classification loop, execution order, run record and refusal logic are untouched. Pre-existing build assertions 17.2 / 18b / 18c / 27.25 / 27.27 / 27.29 stayed green.

persistedStageStatusDecision.decision: The persisted `stageStatus` stores the CASCADED view.
reasoning: Consistency by construction beats consistency by convention. The alternative — persist raw freshness and require every reader to cascade — is exactly the arrangement that produced this defect: the cascade lived at one call site and three others silently skipped it. Nothing in the type system or the schema would have caught a fourth reader forgetting, and no test did.

The cascaded view is the honest answer to the question stageStatus is read to answer. src/release/gate.ts:44 derives PRODUCTION_READY partly from `stageStatus.production.status === "fresh"`. Under the raw view a project whose content stage is stale could still report production as fresh, so a project awaiting a full rebuild could be derived PRODUCTION_READY. Under the cascaded view it cannot.

Nothing is lost. The raw per-stage signal is still fully recoverable from the record: a cascade-only stage carries `reasons` containing exactly "upstream stage <dep> will be rebuilt" and NOT "stage inputs changed since the artifact was produced" or "artifact bytes drifted from the recorded hash". Check 27P.3 asserts that discrimination on a stage (theme) that is stale for no other reason.

No stored artifact is invalidated. stageStatus is recomputed from disk on every load path (refreshStageStatuses re-hashes and re-derives); the persisted copy is a report, never an input to its own recomputation. Every release-project.json already on disk still parses, validates and re-derives identically.
persistedStageStatusDecision.guaranteeIfARawViewWereEverNeeded: It is not needed today, and no reader asks for one. If one ever does, the seam is `propagateStaleStages` being a separate exported function over a caller-owned record — a reader would call refreshStageStatuses's internals rather than re-implementing a cascade. That is a deliberate future seam, not a current code path.

defect1_planOmittedTheCascade.residualDisagreementNotFixed: A FROZEN stage that is stale is classified differently by the two surfaces even though the stage SET agrees: build.ts:129-133 files it under BLOCKED BY "frozen-stage-input-drift" (and then refuses the build), while plan.ts renders it under "STALE (will re-run on release:build)" — which is wrong for a frozen stage, since build refuses rather than re-runs it. This is a distinct defect from the one assigned, it is a label not a stage set (checks 27P.1/27P.2 still hold), and plan.ts is being edited concurrently by the brand agent, so it is reported as a follow-up rather than fixed here.

defect2_unmatchedResolutionFieldWasInvis.symptom: A resolution pack whose routeContent slot values bind to no open requirement produced `matched: []` AND `unmatchedFields: []` — the operator's authored value appeared in neither column of the release:resolve summary.

The field is now reported as unmatched, which resolve.ts renders as "matched no open requirement (recorded, still applied where consumable)" — the accurate description: the value IS still folded into authored.slotValues and still ships.

limitations: 27R.1-27R.5 exercise the synthetic release fixture (data/release-fixture.example). No existing data/ run directory was written: the real projects were read only, and the row-by-row closure measurement ran in the scratchpad against the imported module.

27R.3 passes both with and without the closure (the theme row was already hand-closed), so it is a non-regression guard rather than a detector. 27R.1 and 27R.2 are the checks that fail on a reverted closure.

The three-surface agreement is asserted at two points in the fixture flow (a routeContent-bearing pack and a theme pack) on states where the stale set happens to be exactly the invalidated set. It is not a universal identity — a project that is ALSO stale for an unrelated reason (artifact drift) would legitimately make plan's set a superset of resolve's, and the checks do not model that case.

The frozen-stage wording alignment changes plan's rendered text and NEXT ACTIONS only. PlanView.stale still lists the frozen stage, so a programmatic consumer reading `stale` still sees it as stale rather than blocked; only the operator-facing surface distinguishes them.
followUps: Consider extending planBuildAgreement to compare the per-stage VERDICT KIND (rerun / refuse / reuse) rather than the stage set, which would make the frozen-stage wording alignment machine-enforced instead of asserted through rendered text. This was the plan-cascade agent's followUp[0]; 27R.4 closes the operator-visible half of it, not the structural half.

release:prepare and release:build print no invalidation summary of their own, so the three-surface agreement covers the three surfaces that DO report one. If a fourth reporting surface is added (e.g. a Visual Editor status pane), it must consume invalidatedStages / refreshStageStatuses rather than re-deriving, and should be added to resolvePlanBuildAgreement.

PlanView could expose the staleFrozen / staleRerun split as fields so a consumer of the API (not just the rendered text) can tell a pending rerun from a refusal; not done here because it changes the PlanView contract, which is outside a wording fix.
